analysis.one_liner: Speeds up federal approval of energy projects, removes environmental review rules, and ends electric vehicle tax credits.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee; with no cosponsors and no floor vote, it died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have forced federal agencies and the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to approve or deny energy project permits within 60 days. It would rescind President Biden's climate executive order, write into law the Trump-era rollback of environmental review rules under the National Environmental Policy Act and the narrowed definition of protected waters, remove presidential permits for cross-border pipelines, and let states take over permitting for oil and gas development on federal land. It would also end the tax credit for new electric vehicles after 2022.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas producers, pipeline companies, and natural gas exporters gain the most: mandatory 60-day permit decisions, no presidential permit needed for cross-border pipelines, and the option for states to take over federal-land permitting all speed up project approval. Energy project developers generally benefit from faster, harder-to-challenge approvals. Electric car buyers and existing federal environmental review protections are the clear losers.

how_it_helps.text: It would require federal agencies and FERC to approve or deny every pending and future energy permit application within 60 days, with detailed written explanations to Congress for any denial — sharply limiting the time available for environmental review and public comment.

It would bar presidential permits for cross-border oil and gas pipelines and electric transmission lines, moving that approval to an Act of Congress, and would delegate authority to permit oil and gas development on federal land to state governments that request it.

It would rescind Executive Order 13990 (the climate and public health executive order), permanently codify the 2020 NEPA rollback rule and the Navigable Waters Protection Rule narrowing federal water protections, and end the $7,500 electric vehicle tax credit after 2022.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people living near energy projects bear more risk from rushed 60-day permit decisions with limited environmental review, since the bill also locks in weakened NEPA rules and rescinds the climate executive order. States and tribes lose a federal check on oil and gas development on public land. Electric vehicle buyers pay more without the tax credit.
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities near energy projects; EV buyers

drawbacks.text: The bill terminates the federal tax credit for new plug-in electric vehicles for any vehicle acquired after the end of 2022, raising the effective price of electric cars for buyers.

It would rescind Executive Order 13990 — the order directing federal agencies to act on climate and public health — and permanently write into law the 2020 rollback of the National Environmental Policy Act rules, weakening the environmental review process for federal projects.

It would remove presidential permits for cross-border oil and gas pipelines and electric lines, taking that decision away from the executive and leaving it to Congress, and it would delegate permitting for oil and gas development on federal land to state governments.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's costs to the public are real: undoing the climate executive order, locking in the weakened NEPA and water rules, and speeding permits would mean more fossil fuel development and less environmental review on public land. The benefit claimed — faster approvals and more domestic energy — would flow mostly to producers and developers, and speeding a 60-day clock gives agencies little room to weigh harms honestly. On top of that, the bill went nowhere, so none of its promised benefits were ever delivered.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Rick Scott introduced the bill on March 31, 2022, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor, and no further action was ever recorded on the bill.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill died in committee without ever reaching the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The bill died without a vote, so the status quo held: environmental review requirements and the electric vehicle tax credit remained in place, and oil and gas producers gained nothing they did not already have.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo held; no one gained

for.name: Sen. Rick Scott
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole sponsor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors in either party, and died in the Democratic-controlled Finance Committee without any recorded vote.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and pipeline companies
industries.note: The bill forces 60-day permit decisions, removes presidential permits for cross-border pipelines, and lets states take over permitting on federal land — all aimed at getting oil and gas projects approved faster. Faster approvals mean more drilling, more pipelines, and more revenue for these companies.

industries.industry: Natural gas exporters and LNG terminal developers
industries.note: Liquefied natural gas export terminals and interstate gas pipeline projects are among the permit categories that would get mandatory 60-day decisions. That speeds construction of export facilities that sell gas to foreign buyers.

The bill ends the federal tax credit for new electric vehicles purchased after 2022, making electric cars more expensive for consumers and cutting into the incentive structure automakers have built around the credit.

The fast permit clock covers renewable energy projects too, which these developers would welcome. But the same bill weakens the environmental review process and rescinds the climate executive order, tilting the overall policy landscape back toward fossil fuels.
